{
  "document_classification": {
    "is_summary_style": false,
    "is_full_incident_report": true,
    "contains_multiple_independent_incidents": false,
    "requires_incident_split": false,
    "recommended_output_mode": "single_incident",
    "classification_reason": "The document is a CSB Safety Bulletin centered on one main incident at Praxair St. Louis, with substantial narrative sections including Summary, Incident Description, Emergency Response, Community Impact, Facility Damage, and Incident Analysis/Incident Scenario. Although it references similar incidents in Phoenix, Tulsa, and Fresno, those are comparative examples within the analysis rather than fully developed independent incident narratives in this document."
  },
  "incidents": [
    {
      "incident_id": "incident_1",
      "is_independent_incident": true,
      "time_reference": "June 24, 2005; about 3:20 pm",
      "incident_summary_section": {
        "section_title": "Summary",
        "text": "When exposed to high temperatures and direct sunlight,
propylene cylinders can spontaneously vent through their
relief devices, in turn releasing propylene, which when
ignited, can heat surrounding cylinders and cause them to vent, creating
a domino effect that spreads the fire. This is what occurred on June 24,
2005 at Praxair’s gas filling and distribution facility in St. Louis,
Missouri. A small fire from one propylene cylinder spread to others and
then to propane and acetylene cylinders. Exploding cylinders flew up to
800 feet, damaged property, and started fires in the community. The fire
could not be extinguished until most of the flammable gas cylinders were
expended.

The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) issues
this Safety Bulletin to focus attention on the propylene gas cylinder
hazards that contributed to the fire and explosions at the Praxair facility
and specific actions that propylene gas vendors can take to prevent
similar incidents, which include:
z Installing deluge systems or fixed fire nozzles to cool cylinders in case
of a fire;
z Providing barriers to limit fire spread; and
z Using flammable gas detectors in storage areas to provide early
detection of venting cylinders."
      },
      "incident_description_section": {
        "section_title": "Incident Description",
        "text": "St. Louis was experiencing a heat
wave with bright sunlight and
temperatures reaching 97o
F (36o
C)
on June 24, 2005. Praxair
operations proceeded normally
during the morning and early
afternoon; however, about 3:20 pm,
a technician retrieving cylinders
from an outside storage area saw a
ten-foot high flame coming from a
cylinder (Figure 3) and activated
the fire alarm. Security camera
video from the facility shows the
release and ignition of gas from a
cylinder in the propylene return
area.

Praxair divided the cylinder
storage into “full” and “empty” or
“returned” sections. The
“returned” section, where the fire
originated, is for cylinders returned
for refilling, which may not always
be empty when returned."
      },
      "other_related_sections": [
        {
          "section_title": "Emergency Response",
          "text": "The St. Louis Fire Department
arrived at about 3:35 pm; by this
time, a large number of flammable
gas cylinders were already
involved in the fire. With
explosions propelling cylinders in
all directions inside and outside
the facility, firefighters set up a five-block perimeter, evacuated local
residents, directed a water stream
on the fire, and extinguished
secondary fires started by cylinders
propelled offsite. The fire was
finally controlled at about 8:30 pm."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "Community Impact",
          "text": "Dozens of cylinders and cylinder
parts were propelled into the
community and were found on
sidewalks, front yards, backyards,
courtyards, parking lots, and under
cars. Damage included a burned-
out empty commercial building,
fire-damaged cars, a three-foot hole
in the wall of one residential
building, broken windows, and
other destruction to residential and
commercial buildings. Cylinder
parts traveled as far as 800 feet
from the area of the explosions
(Figure 5). The fire plume spread
asbestos1
 from ruptured acetylene
cylinders over a 1/3-mile wide and
1-mile long area.2

The St. Louis Chief Medical
Examiner attributed the death of
one St. Louis resident to an asthma
attack triggered by noxious smoke
and fumes from the incident.3"
        },
        {
          "section_title": "Facility Damage",
          "text": "While the facility was damaged
extensively by fire and water, 22
employees and two customers
evacuated safely in accordance
with Praxair’s procedures. A
corner of the main production
building and store area was
heavily fire-damaged. Inside, the
office and store areas were water-
and smoke-damaged. In all, the fire
consumed nearly the entire
inventory of flammable gas, or
about 8,000 cylinders."
        },
        {
          "section_title": "Incident Analysis

Incident Scenario",
          "text": "The CSB used physical evidence,
surveillance video recording,
interviews, and information from
Praxair’s internal investigation to
establish the likely failure
sequence:

z Direct sunlight and radiant heat
from asphalt paving heated
returned propylene cylinders;
z High ambient temperature
limited natural air-cooling of the
cylinders;
z The returned cylinders,
containing less gas than full
cylinders, heated at a faster rate
than full cylinders;
z As the cylinder wall
temperatures rose, the internal
pressures increased causing the
relief device on a cylinder valve
to open and vent propylene;
z The venting propylene ignited
(most likely from a static
discharge) at about 3:20 pm;
z An adjacent cylinder, further
heated by the fire, released
propylene, and caught fire;
z An employee saw the fire and
activated the fire alarm;
z All 22 employees and two
customers evacuated;
z The growing fire heated
additional cylinders, which
released more propylene into the
fire;
z The fire’s intensity continued to
raise cylinder temperatures,
softening the steel and rupturing
the cylinders;
z The fire spread to a group of
acetylene cylinders;
z The liquefied petroleum gas4
(LPG)
area of the facility became
fully involved in the fire;
z Ruptured cylinders (acetylene,
propane, and propylene)
rocketed into the community,
damaging buildings and starting
several vehicle fires;5
z St. Louis Fire Department
arrived at about 3:35 pm,
established an unmanned water
spray on the fire, and retreated to
a safe distance. The fire
department did not actively fight
the main fire due to the danger of
rocketing cylinders;
z The Fire Department gained
control of the fire at about 8:30
pm, after the fire had consumed
most of the flammable gases
onsite."
        }
      ],
      "extraction_notes": "Extracted the main incident sections for the Praxair St. Louis event. Omitted figure captions and page headers/footers. Did not treat the 'Similar Incidents' section as separate incidents because they are brief comparative references within the analysis, not fully developed independent incident entries in this document."
    }
  ]
}

accident_scenario_schema_definition:
SCHEMA DEFINITION

The output must strictly follow the provided JSON schema. Each field has a specific meaning and must be filled according to the rules below.

General Rules

Evidence

The "evidence" field must contain a short quote copied directly from the source that supports the extracted value.

If source = "incident_description":
The evidence must be copied verbatim from the incident report text.

Do not invent, paraphrase, or infer evidence.

If no supporting evidence can be found, set:
evidence = "N/A"
source = "Not specified".

Source

The "source" field indicates where the information was obtained, the allowed source are listed in each nodes.

Allowed values:

incident_description  
Information directly extracted from the incident report.


Not specified  
Used when the information cannot be determined from the incident report or reliable external knowledge sources.

Node ID

Each node must include a `node_id`, which serves as a unique identifier in the graph.

The `node_id` must follow the prefix corresponding to the node type:

- H#  → HazardConsequence nodes
- En# → Entity nodes
- C#  → Condition nodes
- Ev# → Event nodes

Where # is a sequential integer starting from 1 within each node category.

Examples:
H1, En1, C1, Ev1

Rules:
- Each node must have exactly one `node_id`.
- All `node_id` values must be unique within the output.
- The prefix must match the node's `node_type`.
- Do not invent other ID formats.
- The `node_id` is only an identifier and must not contain semantic meaning.

--------------------------------------------------
Material
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The hazardous substance involved in the accident scenario.

This refers to the chemical or material present in the process that participates in the release, dispersion, ignition, or hazard consequence.


--------------------------------------------------
Location
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical place or equipment where the accident-related event occurs.

This may include process units, storage tanks, pipelines, packaging areas, or other facility locations relevant to the accident.


--------------------------------------------------
Phase
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The physical phase of the material at the time of the accident.

This condition describes whether the material exists as liquid, vapor, solid, or a two-phase mixture, which can influence release behavior and hazard consequences.


--------------------------------------------------
Temperature
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The temperature condition of the material or environment during the accident scenario.

Temperature can affect vapor generation, chemical stability, and the likelihood of ignition or hazardous reactions.

--------------------------------------------------
Pressure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The pressure condition of the material or process system during the accident scenario.

Pressure influences the containment, release rate, and phase behavior of the material.
Elevated pressure can increase the driving force for a release and accelerate discharge from equipment, while low or atmospheric pressure conditions may affect vapor formation and dispersion behavior.

--------------------------------------------------
Volatility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The tendency of a substance to vaporize.

High volatility substances can easily form flammable or toxic vapor clouds that may contribute to explosion or dispersion hazards.


--------------------------------------------------
Combustibility
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material is capable of burning in the presence of an ignition source.

Combustible materials can participate in fires or explosions when mixed with air and exposed to ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ToxicSubstance
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the material has toxic properties that can cause harm to humans or the environment.

Toxic substances may produce hazardous exposure through vapor dispersion or direct contact.


--------------------------------------------------
Asphyxiant
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
Whether the substance can cause oxygen displacement or interfere with oxygen transport in the body.

Asphyxiants may lead to suffocation or oxygen deficiency hazards in confined or poorly ventilated spaces.


--------------------------------------------------
Conductivity
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The electrical conductivity property of the material.

Low conductivity liquids may accumulate static electricity during transfer operations, increasing the risk of static discharge ignition.


--------------------------------------------------
ReleaseType
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The manner in which hazardous material is released into the environment.

This condition distinguishes between instantaneous releases and continuous releases, which influence dispersion behavior and accident escalation.


--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The source of energy that can ignite a flammable mixture.

Examples include static electricity sparks, open flames, hot surfaces, electrical equipment, or mechanical sparks.


--------------------------------------------------
Confinement
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The degree to which flammable or hazardous material is enclosed within a confined space.

High confinement can increase explosion overpressure and significantly influence explosion severity.


--------------------------------------------------
Dispersion
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The spreading of released material into the surrounding environment.

Dispersion determines how vapors, gases, or toxic substances distribute in air and whether hazardous concentrations can form.


--------------------------------------------------
MechanicalFailure
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
A physical failure of equipment that contributes to the accident.

This may include rupture, leakage, seal failure, structural failure, or malfunction of process equipment that leads to loss of containment.

If a mechanical failure clearly occurred and contributed to the accident,
but the exact failed component or exact failure mode cannot be determined
from the incident description, use "Unknown mechanical failure" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether a mechanical failure should be represented at all.

--------------------------------------------------
InitiatingEvent
--------------------------------------------------

Definition
The first abnormal operational or physical event
that directly initiates the accident sequence
within the process system.

The initiating event may summarize closely related
operational actions and conditions that immediately
lead to the hazardous sequence.

--------------------------------------------------
IgnitionSource Special Rule
--------------------------------------------------

If ignition clearly occurred in the incident, but the exact ignition source
cannot be determined from the incident description, use
"Unknown ignition source" as the name.

Use "Not specified" only when the incident description does not provide enough
support to identify whether an ignition source should be represented at all.
